battle.name: 第三次馬其頓戰爭
battle.brief: 公元前171至168年，第三次馬其頓戰爭是羅馬借仲裁塞琉古王位糾紛之機、攻滅馬其頓王國的戰爭。168年6月22日兩軍在皮埃里亞平原的皮德納決戰：馬其頓方陣正面未崩，卻因右翼指揮官陣亡、側翼遭輕步兵射擊與騎兵衝撞而瓦解。卡面秦弩不在此戰現場，它卻是同一時代東亞的對應物：秦國把弩機大量配給北方邊防步兵，在塹壕後壓制匈奴騎兵，與希臘人的弩砲、羅馬人的標槍同屬一條兵器技術路線。

kit.name: 秦弩
kit.history: 弩機把拉力存起來，射速遠勝拉弓。守城的一方靠它把攻城的人壓在牆外。

countries: 第三次馬其頓戰爭（公元前171至168年）表面上是一場由羅馬仲裁塞琉古王位繼承而引起的戰爭，實際上決定了希臘化世界最後一個獨立王國的存亡。羅馬一方是共和國的執政官與元老院：執政官在任內須先以「特使」身分赴希臘執行任務，戰事爆發後再以帶兵的執政官身分進入戰場；兵員由羅馬軍團、社會戰後編入的意大利同盟軍團，以及盟邦提供的輔助部隊組成，兩支三列槳戰艦的艦隊則負責封鎖愛琴海北岸與馬其頓沿岸的海路，埃托利亞同盟、帕加馬王國與羅得島先後派兵助羅馬。塞琉古一方是安提柯王朝的塞琉古王國，此時正深陷安提柯四世死後的內戰，只掌握東部領土，能派出的援軍規模有限，真正能提供地面部隊的是馬其頓王國。馬其頓國王珀耳修斯站在塞琉古一方，但他的營內並不團結：一批「計算派」臣僚主張先與羅馬討價還價，另一批人則認定羅馬的仲裁書等於一紙亡國令，於是擁護國王全面開戰。羅馬之所以選在馬其頓開刀而不直接攻塞琉古本土，是因為塞琉古太大、離得太遠，而馬其頓小、位置好、又已經站到羅馬的對面；拿下馬其頓，等於拔掉塞琉古伸向希臘的一根手指頭。
countriesEn: The Third Macedonian War (171-168 BC) began on the surface as a war provoked by Roman arbitration over the Seleucid succession, but in reality it decided the survival of the last independent kingdom of the Hellenistic world. On the Roman side stood the consuls and the Senate of the republic: a consul in office first had to travel to Greece on special assignment, and only after the fighting began did he enter the field as a consular commander; the troops were Roman legions, Italian allied formations incorporated after the Social War, and contingents supplied by allied states, while two fleets of triremes blockaded the northern Aegean and the coast of Macedonia so that no relief could land. The Aetolian League, the kingdom of Pergamon and Rhodes sent troops to Rome's side. On the Seleucid side stood the Seleucid Empire of the Antigonid dynasty, then deep in civil war after the death of Antiochus IV: it held only the eastern provinces and could field limited reinforcements, and the power that really supplied ground troops was the kingdom of Macedon. King Perseus of Macedon lined up with the Seleucids, but his own camp was not united: one group of 'calculating' courtiers argued for haggling with Rome first, while another group held that the Roman award was already a death warrant for the kingdom and therefore backed the king in open war. Rome chose to strike at Macedon rather than invade Seleucid territory directly because Seleucid Syria was too large and too far away, whereas Macedon was small, well placed, and had already lined up on Rome's opposite side. Taking Macedon meant cutting off one of the fingers that Seleucid power extended into Greece.
people: The central figure was Perseus, king of Macedon, a distant branch of the Antigonid house who took the throne about 179 BC. At first he was the puppet of the 'calculating' ministers who had put his father on the throne; he married a Seleucid princess and backed Demetrius II in the Seleucid succession, only to have the Roman award of 171 BC rule that he had no claim to the Seleucid throne. That same year he sent his brother Demetrius to Rome with pleas; the Romans kept Demetrius on the far side of the Adriatic as a hostage and cut off the royal house's line of appeal to anyone abroad. Perseus then mustered troops and opened his borders, letting about ten thousand Romans walk into southern Macedon without resistance, thereby turning himself from a party to an arbitration into an enemy of Rome. Three men matter on the Roman side: the consul who commanded the front in 171 BC, Aulus Gnaeus Manlius Vulso, whose reputation suffered when Perseus raided his camp by night; the consul who took over in 168 BC and won, Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, who insisted on rest and reorganisation and turned the expeditionary army into a force that could fight in the field and lay siege; and above both the Senate, which dispatched a tribunal of envoys - Gnaeus Octavius, Gnaeus Cornelius Merula and Lucius Aemilius Macedo - to act as judges. On the Macedonian side stood the king's brother Demetrius, the king's son Philippus, and Minnion who commanded the cavalry. On the day of Pydna Philippus and Demetrius were both killed, and the king escaped with only a few thousand horsemen. On the Seleucid side Antiochus IV was already dead, and the real hand was played by Sosibius, the Seleucid minister who moved between the court and Rome, and by Eumenes II of Pergamon, Rome's most valuable ally, who at the same time embodied Rome's hatred of the Antigonid house because he was the sworn enemy of Antiochus IV.

kits: The Chinese crossbow on this card was not present on the field at Pydna, and that has to be said plainly: the Greek world of the second century BC had no Chinese-style metal-trIGGER crossbow. The missile weapons of Hellenistic armies were the bow, the javelin, and above all the siege artillery - the catapult and the onager - worked by trained engineers; Macedonian and Seleucid infantry carried the sarissa and small round shields, the phalanx was the core of their armies, and the real siege technology of the Hellenistic kingdoms was the counterweight and torsion artillery, operated by dedicated sappers. The Chinese crossbow followed a different technical path: it stored the drawn power in a metal trigger mechanism, so the archer never had to hold the string back to his ear, which meant it could be fired from behind cover, from a wall top, from a tree or from a cart bed, and fired repeatedly. From the Warring States period to the Qin, the crossbow was the principal ranged arm of Chinese infantry; excavated Qin legal texts contain regulations on the specification and the registration of crossbow mechanisms and bolts, which shows that the Qin state treated the crossbow as a standard piece of equipment that could be inspected and replenished, and it was Qin crossbowmen massed behind ramparts and passes who held down Xiongnu cavalry on the northern frontier. As for the tactical position of the crossbow in this war, it corresponds roughly to what the artillery did for the Greeks in siege operations, except that one defends and the other attacks. The equipment actually opposite it on the field of Pydna was Roman: the soft-shanked heavy javelin, the pilum, the short sword, the large shield, the skirmishing javelin of the velites, and cavalry for the flank - the Roman turmae of centre-horse, Numidian horsemen, and Cretan archers. Roman siege equipment included the battering ram, the siege tower, the wooden boarding bridge (the corvus) and the ditch, products of exactly the same engineering-technical ferment as the Greek catapults of the fourth and third centuries BC. One more Macedonian equipment problem is often overlooked: the sarissa needs a great deal of room, and it must be spaced well apart from cavalry, which is the physical reason for the Macedonian defeat at Pydna.

tactics: The tactics of the Third Macedonian War fall into three phases. In 171 BC the Roman army crossed the Adriatic; while marching through the Macedonian highlands its soldiers were bitten by wolves, which the army read as a bad omen, and the operation that actually set the tempo was the narrow defile of the Daynyls Pass, where the Roman column was strung out, the baggage train and the rearguard were harried by Macedonian light horse, and the Romans had to push straight through in a deep column covered by cavalry before they could open a road to the royal capital. In 169 BC Perseus attacked the Roman camp by night and panicked it completely; Vulso recovered the position only by concentrating his cavalry and counterattacking, and that was the background to Rome's decision to send a different commander. The battle of Pydna on 22 June 168 BC is the model of the whole war: the Roman army marched out before dawn, walked for several hours, and engaged at about midday, with about two thousand cavalry on each wing and, in the centre, infantry maniples drawn up in three lines and in deep columns that collided head-on with the Macedonian phalanx; the Roman centre was pushed back for a time and held only because of the thickness of the close-ordered column, in which shield and sword braced like a wall. The real breach was not frontal. When the commanders of the right wing of the phalanx were killed, gaps opened in the formation; Roman light infantry and archers shot into the exposed flanks, and the Roman cavalry - regular turmae together with allied horse - charged into the flank and rear of the phalanx. Once a column on the flank is being shot at and ridden down it can no longer turn as a unit, and the phalanx dissolved into individual long-spear men fighting on their own. In the pursuit the Roman cavalry drove the broken troops to the city walls, and the Macedonian line was finished. The real tactical core of the Roman war effort, however, was the camp system: square camps, ditches, palisades, marching camp laid out by the column of march, which allowed an expeditionary army to wait out three campaigning seasons in the mountains with no supply line, and then to decide the war with a single pitched battle.

data: On numbers the ancient sources contradict one another, so only a rough picture is possible. At the battle of Pydna in 168 BC the Macedonians had about twenty thousand foot and six thousand horse, of whom only some three thousand could be brought into line because of the ground; the Roman figures commonly given are about forty thousand foot and six thousand horse, while Polybius, counting what was actually in the battle line, gives twenty thousand foot and two thousand cavalry engaged, the rest being in camp. The engagement ran from the march out of camp before dawn to contact around midday, a matter of several hours. On losses Polybius estimates that of twenty thousand Macedonian infantry about ten thousand were killed and more than ten thousand taken prisoner, the king himself escaping with only a few thousand horsemen; the Roman casualty figures differ sharply between Livy and Polybius, but all stress that they were far smaller than the enemy's. On duration: the Romans marched out in 171 BC, fought the decisive action at Pydna on 22 June 168, and the Senate declared Macedon 'free' in 167 BC, so roughly four years from the opening of hostilities to the political settlement. The settlement after the war has a set of checkable figures: Macedon was divided into four autonomous districts, the Romans took the revenue of the silver and copper mines, one thousand young men of the nobility were summoned to Rome as hostages, and Macedonians previously declared enemies of the state were put to death, the number being given as three thousand in later accounts. As for booty, Perseus's treasure was carried back to Rome in bulk, and at the triumph of Servius in 167 BC crowds saw for the first time masses of bronze, ivory, gold and silver plate, a display Romans had previously known only from legend. Geographically Pydna lies on the plain of Pieria at the western foot of Mount Olympus, close to the sea and far from the Roman supply base at Brundisium, and that distance was the central logistical difficulty of the expedition.

cause: The trigger lay in the Seleucid Empire, not in Macedon. When Antiochus IV died in 164 BC his young son Antiochus V was set aside, and his elder son Demetrius II competed for the throne with a distant kinsman, Alexander Balas, who was acknowledged by Ptolemy VI of Egypt; at the same time the Ptolemaic kingdom was tearing itself apart, for Ptolemy VIII killed his brother in Alexandria and seized the Egyptian crown, and Egypt called on Rome for help. Rome then placed itself in the chair of the arbiter: in 172 BC it sent the envoys Octavius, Merula and Macedo to adjudicate between the Seleucid and the Egyptian claims. The award went against Demetrius II and, still more, against the Macedonians who had supported him: Rome recognised Demetrius II as Seleucid king and denied Perseus any claim to the Seleucid throne. For the 'calculating' party in Macedon this was tantamount to a death sentence, because Macedon's long policy had been to sit on the fence between Seleucid and Roman power and profit from it; for King Perseus the award was merely a death warrant awaiting execution. In 171 BC he detained the envoys, detained his own brother Demetrius, and opened his borders to the Roman army, buying time for further bargaining while also appealing south to the Seleucid court. The deeper cause lay in Roman strategy in the Mediterranean: Antiochus IV had sought to restore Seleucid hegemony over Greece and had even marched against Egypt, and Rome had to dismantle the Seleucid network in Greece while the empire was in civil war. Macedon was simply the piece that could be cut off most easily. To Rome the war was the execution of an award; to Macedon it was the defence of the state's existence.

impact: The consequences of this war reached beyond Greece. The kingdom of Macedon ceased to exist, with Perseus its last king; Rome did not install a puppet but declared Macedon 'free', cut it into four autonomous districts, placed it under governors, took the mining rights to the silver and copper, and forbade the cities to make alliances or coin money of their own. The Seleucid Empire survived as a state but never again possessed the strength to contest Roman supremacy, and there appeared in the eastern Mediterranean a power with no rival. The Greek cities were drawn one by one into the Roman system of client states, and they were not grateful: the loss of autonomy turned their resentment against Rome, and the Aetolian League and after it the Achaean League became Rome's enemies in Greece, ending in the Roman war against Corinth in 146 BC, the same year in which Carthage and Corinth fell and Rome acquired the Mediterranean world. At that level the Third Macedonian War was the largest single expansion of the late Roman republic: it settled the question of who would decide the fate of Greece, and the answer was no longer Persia, nor the Seleucids, nor Macedon, but Rome. A second layer of consequence lies in military organisation: Rome's accumulation of experience in distant campaigns and in pitched battle established the standing expeditionary army commanded by a consul together with the engineering that supported it; the techniques of the Hellenistic armies - the phalanx of many nations, the catapult, the cavalry - flowed into Rome through prisoners, deserters and conscripted Greek craftsmen. The parallel in the history of weapons lies in Asia: in the same century the Qin army was massing crossbowmen behind ramparts on the northern frontier to hold down the Xiongnu, and the crossbow, by storing the drawn power, let troops with no long training in the bow fire steadily from behind a ditch - the other end of the same technical line on which the Greeks broke cities with artillery and the Romans broke phalanxes with the pilum.

result: The battle of Pydna on 22 June 168 BC decided the war. The Macedonian phalanx did not break in front; it broke on the flank. The king's son Philippus and his brother Demetrius were killed in turn, the cavalry commander Minnion was scattered, and Perseus himself escaped with a few thousand horsemen, falling back towards the royal capital Pella and the harbour. Rome then blockaded the Macedonian coast, and with no way out Perseus took a mountain road to the island of Samothrace, where he was taken in by the Roman naval commander Gnaeus Octavius - the general who not long before had been a guest in the king's own court, and who nevertheless received the order to take the prisoner. Perseus surrendered in 168 BC and was brought to Rome the following year, stripped of his kingship and of his freedom, and he died of illness while under guard. In 167 BC the Roman Senate formally declared Macedon 'free': the kingdom was abolished, the land divided into four autonomous districts under Roman governors, the treasury and the mines taken over, the young nobles summoned to Rome, and a number of those declared enemies of the state executed. The war ended in a complete Roman victory. It did not take Perseus's life in the field, but it took the state of Macedon, the possibility of Seleucid primacy in Greece, and the margin by which the Greeks might have decided their own fate. Servius's triumph displayed the booty in the streets of Rome, and with it the Third Macedonian War came to its close; the Fourth Macedonian War would break out more than twenty years later, until in 146 BC the freedom of Greece was cancelled for good.
